core_claim: A theory specifies what constructs matter, how they relate, why, and under which conditions.
Constructs, data, and inferences must be aligned at the same level or explicitly linked across levels.
business_use: Avoiding ecological fallacies in people analytics

core_claim: Mediators explain how an effect occurs. Moderators specify when and for whom it occurs.
business_use: Targeting interventions to segments and mechanisms

core_claim: Many published findings do not replicate, transparency and pre-registration improve credibility.
business_use: Treating single studies and vendor claims with caution

core_claim: Valuable, rare, inimitable, and organized resources produce sustained competitive advantage.
A resource yields sustained advantage only if it is valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and exploited by the organization.
Firms exist because they integrate specialized knowledge better than markets.
Competition is a disequilibrating struggle for comparative advantage in resources.
Relational and intellectual market-based assets create shareholder value.
Advantage in changing environments comes from sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring resources.
The ability to recognize, assimilate, and apply external knowledge depends on prior related knowledge.
Adaptive systems must balance search for new possibilities with refinement of existing ones.
Firms that structurally or contextually combine exploration and exploitation outperform over time.
business_use: Managing new ventures alongside the core

core_claim: Self-interested agents with private information require monitoring and incentive alignment.
Managers can be pro-organizational stewards, and control can crowd out stewardship.
Governance (market, hybrid, hierarchy) is chosen to economize on transaction costs given asset specificity and uncertainty.
Organizational outcomes reflect the values and cognitive bases of top executives.
Organizations manage dependence on external resource providers through co-optation, alliances, and mergers.
Coercive, mimetic, and normative pressures make organizations in a field similar.
business_use: Anticipating adoption of standards and practices

core_claim: Organizations need pragmatic, moral, and cognitive legitimacy to obtain resources.
business_use: Managing reputation and license to operate

core_claim: Firms create value for, and depend on, multiple stakeholders beyond shareholders.
Environmental selection, not adaptation, drives change in organizational populations.
There is no single best structure, effective structure fits the environment.
Hidden quality causes adverse selection that can unravel markets.
Costly, observable actions credibly reveal hidden quality when costs differ by type.
The uninformed party designs menus that induce self-selection.
Signals are honest when they are handicaps only high-quality senders can afford.
Consumers diverge in identity-relevant domains to avoid signaling undesired identities.
The highest types may refuse to signal because other information already separates them.
Relationships are sustained by reciprocal exchanges of valued resources.
Power derives from structural position in exchange networks.
Weak ties bridge social circles and carry novel information.
business_use: Job search, referrals, and sales prospecting

core_claim: Brokers spanning disconnected groups gain information and control benefits.
Resources embedded in relationships enable action, closure builds trust and norms.
Commitment and trust are key mediating variables in successful relational exchange.
Innovations spread through social systems over time in an S-curve shaped by perceived attributes.
Adoption is driven by innovation (external) and imitation (internal) coefficients.
Attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived control shape intentions and behavior.
Perceived usefulness and ease of use drive intention to use technology.
Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions drive use.
National cultures differ on dimensions such as power distance and individualism.
People seek to reduce power distance to those above and to increase it to those below.
Cultural practices and values differ and shape endorsed leadership styles.
Basic human values form a circular motivational continuum with compatibilities and conflicts.
Cultures differ in the strength of social norms and tolerance of deviance.
Independent and interdependent selves shape cognition, emotion, and motivation.
Motivation is a multiplicative function of expectancy, instrumentality, and valence.
People compare their outcome-to-input ratios with others and act to restore equity.
Specific, difficult goals with feedback raise performance.
Effort accelerates as people approach a goal.
Autonomy, competence, and relatedness fuel intrinsic motivation. Controlling rewards can crowd it out.
Being slightly behind can increase effort and the probability of winning.
People pursue goals with a promotion (gains) or prevention (safety) focus.
Value increases when goal-pursuit means fit one's regulatory orientation.
Psychological distance increases abstract, high-level construal.
Present bias creates conflict between planner and doer selves. Commitment devices help.
People evaluate themselves by comparing with others.
Group memberships form part of the self and drive ingroup favoritism.
Identity balances opposing needs for assimilation and differentiation.
Informational and normative influence lead people to match group behavior.
Descriptive and injunctive norms guide behavior when salient.
The presence of others improves well-learned and impairs novel performance.
Attentional conflict between audience and task drives social facilitation effects.
Fear of isolation suppresses expression of perceived minority opinions.
Decision makers satisfice under cognitive and information limits.
Judgment relies on heuristics that produce systematic biases.
Outcomes are evaluated as gains and losses from a reference point, with loss aversion.
Owners value goods more than non-owners.
People assign money to mental accounts that violate fungibility.
business_use: Bundling, gift cards, and price partitioning

core_claim: Fast intuitive and slow deliberative processes jointly shape judgment.
business_use: Designing for intuitive vs. considered choices

core_claim: People use their feelings as information when making judgments.
Ease of processing feels good and increases liking and perceived truth.
Unexpected fluency is attributed to past experience and produces feelings of familiarity.
How options are presented, including defaults, predictably changes choices.
Positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoires and build lasting resources.
Emotional reactions to life changes fade as people adapt.
Affective states vary along valence and arousal dimensions.
High-arousal emotional content is more likely to be shared.
Emotions arise from appraisals of situations on dimensions such as certainty and control.
Remembered experience is dominated by the peak and the end.
Persuasion follows a central or peripheral route depending on motivation and ability.
Consumers learn persuasion tactics and use that knowledge to cope with them.
People share content that serves impression management, emotion regulation, and social bonding.
Media salience transfers to public salience.
Selecting and emphasizing aspects of reality shapes interpretation.
Audiences actively select media to satisfy needs.
Undirected communication lets people seek interaction without imposing on anyone.
Repeated exposure increases liking.
Positive valence increases perceived familiarity.
Liking peaks at moderate levels of novelty and complexity.
Novel partners renew sexual interest after satiation.
Others' consumption raises (bandwagon) or lowers (snob) demand. Price can raise demand (Veblen).
Women and minorities are more likely to be appointed to precarious leadership positions.
Labor invested in creating a product increases its valuation.
Adding an asymmetrically dominated option increases choice of the target.
Initial values bias subsequent numerical estimates.
Prototypical, average stimuli are judged more attractive.
A blunder can increase the likability of a highly competent person.
Less typical items are judged more similar to typical items than the reverse.
Similar people connect at higher rates than dissimilar people.
People partner with others similar to themselves.
Others both attract (imitation) and repel (differentiation).
Aggregating independent estimates cancels individual errors.
Reporters converge on the same stories and sources.
Olfaction is tightly linked to emotion and autobiographical memory.
Recognition and resources accrue to those already advantaged.
Individuals exert less effort when working collectively.
The presence of others reduces individual helping.
Shared resources are overused unless governed by effective institutions.
Cohesive groups suppress dissent and make defective decisions.
Information flows from sensory to short-term to long-term memory.
Creativity cycles between generating preinventive structures and exploring them.
Novel ideas recombine existing knowledge. Impact peaks with conventional bases plus atypical combinations.
Industry profitability depends on rivalry, entry, substitutes, and buyer and supplier power.
Environmental stimuli shape internal states that drive approach or avoidance.
